title: Loving for others
hook: a friend's good news, a half-second pause, and a hadith that walks straight into it

segments.voice: Yesterday: silat al-rahim, ties joined again even when someone else cut them. Today, a sentence about what you want, and who else you want it for.

A friend gets the job you both applied for. Or the apartment. Or the news you've waited years to hear yourself. The text arrives, and for some people there's a half-second before typing congratulations where something tightens. Nobody chooses that half-second. But a short hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari walks right into it. The Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, says, in paraphrase: none of you truly believes until he loves for his brother what he loves for himself.
screen: `THE FRIEND GETS THE JOB.` → `A HALF-SECOND PAUSE.` → `LOVE FOR HIM WHAT YOU LOVE.`

segments.voice: Look at how the sentence is built. It doesn't say: stop wanting good things. It starts from what a person already wants for himself: health, ease, being forgiven, a good name, rest. Your own wanting is the ruler. Whatever you'd be glad to receive, want it for someone else too. Then the verb. The hadith doesn't say give, or share, though those may follow. It says love: yuhibbu, he loves. It's about what the heart wants. You can't always hand someone what they need. You can always want it for them. Then who counts. The hadith in Bukhari says his brother. A narration in Sahih Muslim gives the same words with his brother, or, the narrator adds, his neighbor. And a narration in al-Nasa'i spells out what kind of thing is meant: of good. Not whatever you happen to crave, but the good: guidance, health, mercy, the thing that would actually help. And the strong opening: none of you believes. Some commentators read this as faith not yet complete, not as a person leaving Islam. The hadith points at a gap between believing in words and believing all the way down, and it finds that gap somewhere very ordinary: what happens inside when someone else gets the good thing. The half-second is where the hadith does its work.
screen: `YOUR OWN WANTING IS THE RULER.` · `YUHIBBU: LOVE, NOT ONLY GIVE.` · `BROTHER, NEIGHBOR: OF GOOD.` · `FAITH, ALL THE WAY DOWN.`

segments.voice: Name one thing you've been hoping for lately, rest, a good result, a door opening, and hold it a moment. Then bring someone to mind, maybe the one whose good news stung a little, and picture them receiving that same thing, staying with it until the wanting feels real, or at least a little closer. If you pray, you can ask for it for them by name, before you ask for yourself.
Loving for others. From the hadith in Bukhari: wanting for another person the good you want for yourself, as part of faith itself. Today's word.
Your line: love it for them. Your own wanting is the ruler. Tomorrow, contentment with little.

howItsDone: Muslims cite this hadith as a measure of faith: wanting for others the good one wants for oneself, and making du'a for others' good.

fork.setup: your friend gets the very thing you were hoping for. the hadith in Bukhari gives you a measure for the next moment. what is it?
options: say nothing until the feeling passes.
want for them what you'd want for yourself.
point out it could just as easily have been you.
fork.reveal: none of you believes until he loves for his brother what he loves for himself: your own wanting becomes the measure for theirs.

original.note: Arabic: he loves. the verb at the heart of the hadith (Bukhari 13).

trapdoor: what you thought: be happy for people.
what it means: want for another person, really want, the good you want for yourself, because that is part of faith.
what a scholar hears: Bukhari 13 with Muslim 45's 'or his neighbor' and al-Nasa'i's 'of good': the circle is wide, and the thing loved is good.

chat.says: My friend got the job I wanted, and I felt a pang. What does Islam say?
options: A hadith says none of you believes till he loves for his brother what he loves for himself.
It says to stop wanting good things for yourself, so the pang can't happen.
It says only to give your friend a gift; what you feel inside doesn't count.
chat.meaning: The hadith starts from your own wanting and asks you to love the same good for others; it's about the heart, not only giving.
